title: Godot Vs JavaScript/html canvas
author: KingofKingsofKingsof
selftext:
What are the advantages or disadvantages of using Godot Vs js for AI dev? So far I've only made js canvas games with AI assistance, and I don't know how to use Godot (I struggled to make the jump from gamemaker to Godot a few years ago). 

  
Thanks

comments.author: phiiiiiiii
comments.body: To put it in layman terms: JS is for practicing, Godot (or Unity, Unreal, etc)... is for getting serious.

comments.author: strange_username58
comments.body: Younare going to want to go with godot

comments.author: thecrownforge
comments.body: If you want a game that opens from a browser link, JS canvas can be a final choice. The hard part as the project grows is keeping state, input and rendering organized. Godot gives you a scene editor and built in animation tools, but you would still need to test its web build on the devices you care about. I would switch only if those tools solve a problem you actually have.

comments.author: BrasilianPianistBoi
comments.body: It depends on MCP quality rn

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
For most games, you’ll get a much better game if you use an engine like Godot. You’ll spend less time and get a better game.

If you use straight JS, your game will be a little easier to host and the file sizes will be smaller. This can be nice for web games. But you will spend a bunch of tokens & time reimplementing stuff that already exists in Godot, and your version probably won’t work as well.

For my recent project I am going JS, because (1) I already made games that way without AI and it’s just the way I prefer to do things, and (2) the game isn’t using many features from Godot.

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body:
I feel like Godot is in this awkward middle ground between browser/threejs and Unreal and Unity. If you’re trying to make a commercial release and especially if you’d like to do console ports it’s probably a much better idea to use Unity or Unreal.

My workflow is to prototype games in threejs and then port to Unreal once they show commercial potential. This is working great with Claude Code. I get the benefits of rapid prototyping in the browser and then a full featured engine for commercial releases that span many platforms.

One thing I do is keep my art pipeline mostly outside of Unreal, so I do full level scenes in blender including collider geometry. I also tell Claude Code to not use blueprints at all and just write C++ and set things up so we can do headless simulation. I also had Claude write itself a helper library for working more efficiently with Unreal.
